stem: A Massachusetts drug store pharmacy holds its ordinary pharmacy license but has never obtained a sterile compounding pharmacy license. It wants to begin preparing patient-specific sterile ophthalmic preparations on site. Which statement best describes the licensure issue?

choices.text: The ordinary drug store license is sufficient whenever each preparation is patient-specific.
The pharmacy may begin immediately and seek a sterile-compounding license only if the Board later inspects it.
The pharmacy needs the applicable sterile compounding pharmacy licensure before engaging in this sterile compounding activity.
Sterile compounding is permitted without additional licensure when no Schedule II-V drug is used.
Sterile compounding licensure applies only to out-of-state pharmacies shipping into Massachusetts.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts separately licenses sterile compounding pharmacy activity. Patient-specific status does not convert an ordinary drug store license into a sterile compounding license, and the current licensure framework includes satisfactory Board inspection before an original sterile compounding license is issued.

choice_analysis.A: Patient-specific status does not make the ordinary license sufficient.
choice_analysis.B: The licensure and inspection gate precedes lawful operation in the specialty category.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: the specialty license is required before the activity begins.
choice_analysis.D: Controlled-substance schedule is not the trigger for sterile-compounding licensure.
choice_analysis.E: Massachusetts also licenses resident sterile compounding pharmacies.

explanation.mpje_trap: Patient-specific compounding does not eliminate the specialty licensure requirement for sterile compounding.

reasoning_steps: Classify the proposed preparation as sterile compounding
Separate ordinary drug-store licensure from the specialty sterile-compounding category
Apply the sterile-compounding licensure gate before operations begin
